title: Begging cabarets for work and learning songs from a player piano
summary: She sneaked out nightly asking clubs to hire her, finally got a chance at Dago Frank's, learned songs from a player piano, and stayed a year and ten months until the police closed it.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Gave me the job peeling potatoes. And so, I peeled the potatoes and stayed there, and in the meantime, I used to -- when I was -- I would sit there and hear them say that girls made $10.00 a week in nightclubs. They didn't call them nightclubs. What did they call them then? I don't know what they called them.
Cabarets?
No, they didn't call them cabarets. They called them -- I think they called them nightclubs.
Uh-huh.

And anyhow, during that time, when I was there, at night I would sneak out while Helen was working. She was tired, the second cook, you know. I'd sneak out and go down to Dago Frank's and the different places and ask them did they want to hire a girl. I didn't know you didn't say that that way. You'd say do you want a singer or something.
I'd say do you want to hire a girl. I meant did they want to hire somebody to sing, you know.
Uh-huh.

And so they'd say, "Get her out of here. My God, I'll get my license taken away from here. Get her out of here." I was so little, you know. And so they'd put me out, each place I'd go. I went to the different places where Birk and Cora Greene and the different ones were working, and they'd make fun of me. But I kept going. You know, I'm very determined. I kept going. I'd go back every night. So finally, I think I sang a song down there, down to Dago Frank's. And the man, Roy, his name was Roy, he was the manager, he said, "Bruce, get her out of here. She's terrible." So he said, "Oh, Roy, give her a chance. You can see she's nothing but a kid, so give her a chance." So he said all right, but still he didn't hire me right then. So I went back, and then in the meantime, instead of staying at Mrs. Love's, I had moved over to 32nd and Dearborn, to a lady named Miss Bern, Cora Dern. And she let me stay there. I think I paid her a dollar a week for a room. A dollar a week for this room. And I stayed there, and one night the telephone rang, and it said come down to Dago Frank's.
Uh-huh.
Come down to Dago Frank's. And I went down there and they let me start to sing. Well, in the

meantime I had heard -- you talk to me about piano again, because this is something else I want to tell you about player pianos. In the meantime, I had heard, all Night Long, 'Where the River Shannon Flows,' on this player piano, and I had heard the words from them.
Uh-huh.

See? So when I went down there I sang those two songs in high soprano, and you know as heavy as my voice is, but what did I know. And I still don't know one note from the other. So I sang all Night Long, and 'Where the River Shannon Flows.' Well, Roy scratched his head and went on back in his office, as if to say, 'Poor girl, I'll let her stay.' So they let me stay. And each day I would learn a song on that player piano.
Uh-huh.
You know? And every night, when I'd go back, I'd sing a different song I had learned off the player piano, you know?
Uh-huh.

And the girls -- they were the sporting girls, you know, and you know they are always very tender hearted, as a rule. They would give me money and then they would make me sing again, and they'd say, 'Now, don't sing it that way. Sing it such and such a way,' you know, and I would sing, and finally I made good. I stayed there a year and ten
months. That's when I went up to Hugh Hoskins.
I see.
That's when I went up to Hugh Hoskins. I stayed a year and ten months, because they closed Dago Frank's.
Oh. Why did they close it?
Because it was nothing but prostitutes there.
Oh. So the police closed it.
The police closed it, see? That's when I went up to Hugh Hoskins. Now, you got that?
